clue.text: (see 21dn.)
Private Eye gets stuck into hawk (plummy Brian)

indicators.note: stuck into means pushed inside, so one part ends up within the other

parts.note: to hawk goods is to sell them
the magazine speaks of itself in the editorial first person plural

explanation.surface: The magazine wades into a quarrel with a bird of prey, in parentheses a posh-voiced Brian.
explanation.walkthrough: The editorial voice goes in after the first two letters of the selling word. Brian Sewell was the London art critic famous for his very plummy accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Sewell, the Evening Standard art critic, was known above all for his ultra-posh drawl.

clue.text: Abstained rashly, without Tony's lead — that's a bit off

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the jumbled letters go round the other part
doing something rashly means doing it carelessly, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written before it is jumbled

indicators.note: a lead is the front position, so only the first letter of the name is used

parts.note: the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: MPs rashly abstain from a vote, defying Tony Blair, and are told that is a bit much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'minus'; it means outside, so the letter is kept and wrapped, not removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is a bit off means it is improper or tasteless, offensive to good manners.

clue.text: Swearing caused by, it's said, an "E" for example

indicators.note: it's said means spoken out loud, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: E is one of the five vowel letters

explanation.surface: Bad language blamed on an E, ecstasy perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted E looks like the drug ecstasy; it is just the letter, an example of a vowel.
explanation.definitionFit: An avowal is a solemn public declaration, so swearing in the sense of making an oath.

clue.text: Some of us ignore the sticking up of two fingers?

definitions.text: the sticking up of two fingers?

indicators.note: some of means a portion, so the letters are a run taken from the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A complaint that people ignore a rude two-fingered gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: Sticking up two fingers, palm inward, is the British V-sign insult, roughly the middle finger elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The rude V gesture is a hand signal, so the question mark marks one example of a gesture.

clue.text: Drives home with erection — blown at Yom Kippur?

definitions.note: describes the noun by what is done with it

parts.note: to ram a point home is to drive it home
the horn is slang for an erection

explanation.surface: A man drives home aroused, then the clue swerves to the Jewish Day of Atonement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown' teases a sexual meaning; it is a trumpet being sounded.
explanation.definitionFit: The shofar, made from the horn of a ram, is sounded in synagogue at the close of Yom Kippur.

clue.text: (see 24dn.)
The main leaders of our country engender another nightmare

indicators.note: leaders are the ones out in front, so only the opening letter of each following word is kept

parts.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A grumble that the country's top politicians are about to bring on yet another nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main leaders' reads as one phrase about chief politicians, but 'The main' is the definition and 'leaders' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is an old poetic name for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main.

clue.text: Grant has sex with a goat's front bit — that shows taste!

parts.note: to grant something is to give it
'it' is a coy word for sex
taken as written

indicators.note: the front bit of a word is its opening, here the first two letters only

parts.note: the first two letters of goat

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of Grant and a goat, with a mock-prim remark about his taste.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Hugh Grant and bad taste; 'taste' is really the verb, to try a little of something.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste something is to sample or try it, which is what the idiom for making an attempt means.

clue.text: Getting leg over once excited, some Scots were infamously knocked off here

definitions.text: some Scots were infamously knocked off here

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Getting your leg over is British slang for sex, so this reads as randy Scots killed in the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked off' looks sexual too; it means killed.
explanation.definitionFit: In the 1692 massacre of the MacDonalds in a Highland glen, government troops murdered dozens of their hosts.

clue.text: Piss artist, for example, backing the hidden aim of a party loan?

definitions.text: the hidden aim of a party loan?

parts.note: to piss is to pee
RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the words for example are written right to left

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: A drunkard is offered as an example in some murky business about a loan to a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piss artist' is British slang for a drunk and wants to be one unit; it splits into two words. The definition recalls the 2006 cash-for-honours row over secret loans to Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenders to a party were suspected of wanting a seat in the House of Lords, a title of nobility, in return.

clue.text: Brenda's place as wife indoors? Slovenly and loveless

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife

indicators.note: something slovenly is untidy and messed about, so the letters are jumbled
love is zero, the letter shaped like a nought, and loveless means without it

parts.note: taken as written before it is altered

explanation.surface: The Queen pictured as a housewife kept at home, untidy and unloved.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. Drop one O from the word indoors, rearrange what is left, and put the wife letter in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Windsor Castle is one of the monarch's official residences, and Windsor is also the royal family's surname.

clue.text: (& 21ac.) Auto-engineered end of member?

parts.note: surface reading: the tip of a limb, or something ruder, built by a car maker
setter's reading: auto means self, so a self-inflicted finish to the career of a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A mechanical engineer's idea of the tip of a man's member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auto' points at cars, but it is the Greek prefix for self; 'member' points at anatomy, but it is an MP.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a career-ending blunder that a politician brings about by their own act.

clue.text: Happy Londoner nursing an erection

indicators.note: nursing means holding close, so the words before it hold the letters inside them

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A cheerful Londoner with an erection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erection' teases the obvious; it is anything erected, a built structure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pylon is a tall steel tower put up to carry power lines, a structure that is erected.

clue.text: It's a piece of shit turning over rifles

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a stool is the medical word for a single faecal motion

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that a thing is rubbish while flipping it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rifles' looks like a noun for guns; here it is the verb, to search and steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To rifle a place is to ransack it for valuables, which is to plunder or pillage it.

clue.text: Unauthorised release of mole: make out journalist plays central role

indicators.note: playing the central role means standing right in the middle of the rest
out here means put out of order, so the two words before it are scrambled together

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
ED, editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A spy's disclosure, with a hack at the centre of the story and some necking on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' reads as snogging or as discerning; it is the word make plus an anagram signal. The journalist sits exactly at the halfway point of the ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A confidential office document passed to the press without permission is an unauthorised release of information.

clue.text: Understands when receiving head from Lewinsky (Monica)

indicators.note: something receiving another thing takes it inside itself

parts.note: to see a point is to understand it

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is all that is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A nod to Monica Lewinsky and the act that made her notorious.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed Monica seems to complete Lewinsky's name; it is the definition, pointing to a different Monica.
explanation.definitionFit: Monica Seles is the tennis champion who won nine Grand Slam singles titles, so the clue names her by first name.

clue.text: Butcher's Women possibly seek to get screwed

parts.note: a toilet door marked Women is one example of a loo

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted out of shape, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A meat seller reports that women go looking to be bedded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's' is Cockney rhyming slang: butcher's hook rhymes with look, so a butcher's is a glance. The possessive makes it look like a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a butcher's and having a quick inspection mean the same thing in British slang.

clue.text: Wrinkly told off Cyclops in the taxman's clutches

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the word before it is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: being in something puts a thing inside it, completed by the clutches that follow
to be held in someone's clutches is to be gripped all round

parts.note: IR is the Inland Revenue, the old UK tax authority
the setter speaking of himself

explanation.surface: An elderly person scolds the setter, who is being squeezed by the tax collector.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told off' wants to mean scolded; 'off' is the anagram signal on the word before it. Wrinkly is British slang for an old person.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrinkly, informally, is an elderly person, the same thing as a veteran who has been around a long while.

clue.text: Material balls

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a soft woven woollen cloth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is British slang for nonsense, not testicles here.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a fabric and, in British usage, empty talk meant to evade or flatter.

clue.text: Florida: caught getting gobbled by tart — erection gone!

parts.note: FL is the postal abbreviation for Florida

indicators.note: something gobbled is swallowed, so it ends up inside whatever does the eating

parts.note: tart in the sense of sour
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A man in Florida, caught with a tart, loses his erection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tart' reads as a prostitute; it is the adjective meaning sour. The caught letter goes just inside the sour word, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaccid means limp and soft, the state of a penis once it is no longer erect.

clue.text: Say Brown's comeback is the action of a pushy type?

definitions.text: the action of a pushy type?

indicators.note: a comeback is a return journey, so the words before it are read from the end

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated e.g.
dun is a dull greyish-brown colour

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's return to power is mocked as the work of a pushy politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown suggests Gordon Brown; it is only the colour. The question mark marks the definition as playful: a pushy person pushes, literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudge is a small push with the elbow, so it is literally what someone pushy does.

clue.text: Unremitting Conservative support on drugs to a point

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
an easel is a stand that supports a painting
E is ecstasy, so Es are ecstasy tablets
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Tory backing for drug use, but only up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To a point' reads as 'somewhat'; it is a link word plus a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unremitting never lets up, so it goes on without stopping or pause.

clue.text: Cameron's entrance sheer crap — laughed at on TV

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for a noun: a show that is laughed at on TV

indicators.note: an entrance is where you come in, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of the name

indicators.note: crap means badly made, so the word before it is put together wrongly

parts.note: taken as written before it is jumbled

explanation.surface: A critic says David Cameron's arrival was pure rubbish, a joke on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheer crap' looks like a single insult; 'sheer' is the fodder and 'crap' tells you to rearrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers was the long-running American sitcom set in a Boston bar, a comedy watched for laughs.

clue.text: Nothing omitted from Brenda's A to Z of Sham

indicators.note: nothing is zero, the letter shaped like a nought, and it is left out of the words that follow

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, and ER is the Queen's royal cipher
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is missing from the Queen's street atlas of a place called Sham.
explanation.walkthrough: An A to Z is a London street atlas, which makes Sham look like a place name; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz means artificial or substitute, an imitation of the real thing, so it is fake.

clue.text: (see 12ac.)
(& 1dn.) Fatso wobbling in to soak butter up

indicators.note: going in to something means entering it, so one part goes inside the other

parts.note: to sop is to soak, as bread sops up gravy

indicators.note: a wobbling thing will not hold its shape, so its letters are shaken up

parts.note: taken as written before it is jumbled

explanation.surface: A wobbly fat man mopping up butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' seems to be the stuff being soaked up; 'butter up' is the definition, meaning to flatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To soft-soap someone is to flatter them to get your way, the same as buttering them up.

clue.text: State involved in fellatio watch?

indicators.note: involved in means caught up inside, so the letters lie within the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A smutty question about watching oral sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Iowa is one of the fifty United States, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Approaches from beneath — "Has orgasm finished?"

parts.note: the slang verb for reaching orgasm
time's up means time is finished

explanation.surface: Someone underneath asks whether their partner has climaxed yet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that rises towards you from below, like a diver surfacing, is approaching from beneath.

clue.text: (+ 7dn.) Bloody awful number one oppressing the underprivileged

indicators.note: in a down clue one part pressing down on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: number one is the nursery euphemism for urinating
the underprivileged are the poor

explanation.surface: A complaint about a leader who grinds down those with least.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' looks like a prime minister or top dog; it is the childish word for a wee.
explanation.definitionFit: Piss-poor is crude British slang for extremely bad, the same force as bloody awful.

clue.text: For nothing on earth is supposedly led by Bush

definitions.note: a descriptive clause: what the answer is said to be, rather than a noun phrase

parts.note: something given for nothing is free
the earth is the world

explanation.surface: A jibe that George W Bush leads the planet to no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'supposedly' is the joke: American presidents are called the leader of the democratic West.
explanation.definitionFit: The US president is routinely styled leader of the democratic Western nations, so Bush nominally headed them.

clue.text: Condoms? China has seconds!

parts.note: rhyming slang: china plate means mate
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A joke that China is going back for a second helping of contraceptives.
explanation.walkthrough: China looks like the country; it is Cockney rhyming slang. Mates was a British condom brand launched by Richard Branson.
explanation.definitionFit: Mates condoms were a well-known UK brand, so the question mark flags a brand name rather than a synonym.
